en.title: Kerbal Space Program's Rocket Fuel: A 2005 Flash Game?
en.summary: The creator of the beloved Kerbal Space Program reveals an unlikely inspiration for the hit space simulator: a promotional Flash game for Top Gear. This unexpected origin story highlights the game's unique development path.
en.body:
When players blast off into the vastness of space in **Kerbal Space Program**, they’re engaging with a game celebrated for its remarkably realistic physics engine. But the journey to creating this beloved title, which has captivated both hardcore and casual gamers since its 2015 launch, began with a surprisingly humble and unexpected source: a promotional Flash game. Felipe Falanghe, the visionary behind **Kerbal Space Program**, recently shared that one of his earliest inspirations came from a lighthearted, browser-based experience.

Falanghe, who now heads his own development company, Floating Origin Interactive, recounted how this particular Flash game, associated with the **Top Gear** franchise, bore a striking resemblance to the core mechanics he was envisioning for **KSP**. "That was the most similar game to KSP that I could find back then," Falanghe stated, reflecting on the game's development. This revelation comes as **Kerbal Space Program** continues to be a standout title, available across major platforms including PC, PlayStation, and Xbox, and is known for its pseudorealistic orbital physics that allow for complex maneuvers like Hohmann transfers and orbital rendezvous. The game's development itself was a leap of faith, born from Falanghe's time at the marketing firm Squad, where a deal was struck: help with projects, and he'd be allowed to pursue his own game idea. This unconventional path led to one of PC gaming's most unique and enduring simulators.

## An Unconventional Spark

Falanghe’s path into game development was paved with early PC experiences, from figuring out **Flight Simulator 4** on his father’s laptop with his brother to exploring the life-simulation possibilities of **The Sims**. These early dives into interactive worlds fostered a love for modding, which directly influenced his own creative ambitions. The decision to pursue **Kerbal Space Program** was made under the assumption that his tenure at Squad might be short-lived, a mindset that encouraged bold creative risks. "I was always working with this idea that for all I know next week this is over, so let's do anything I can under that assumption," he recalled. It's a sentiment that underscores the sheer audacity of pitching the full scope of **KSP** to a traditional game studio, a feat he wisely bypassed by leveraging his unique opportunity.

## The Kerbal Community's Embrace

The **Kerbal Space Program** community is renowned for its dedication and ingenuity, often pushing the game's physics engine to its absolute limits. Players meticulously craft intricate rockets and orbital stations, sharing their triumphs and spectacular failures across forums and social media. The reveal of an inspiration rooted in a simple Flash game only adds another layer of charm to the **KSP** legend, demonstrating that groundbreaking ideas can emerge from the most unexpected corners of the gaming landscape. This connection to a nearly forgotten browser game serves as a testament to the enduring power of innovative game design, regardless of its initial presentation.

## What's Next

While Falanghe is currently focused on new projects with Floating Origin Interactive, the enduring legacy of **Kerbal Space Program** continues to inspire. Fans eagerly await any future developments or expansions for the beloved space simulator, which remains a benchmark for physics-based gameplay.

content_raw: Disk Cleanup (Image credit: Future) Welcome to Disk Cleanup , our regular weekend feature delving into the PCs of PC gaming luminaries. Come back every weekend to read a new interview, digging into the important questions, like "How tidy is your desktop?" and "What game will you never uninstall?" Felipe Falanghe got into PC gaming by playing Flight Simulator 4 on his dad's laptop. "I remember having no idea what I was doing," Falanghe says. "Me and my brother, we were just figuring it out and playing it on the keyboard and trying to make it go." It was through games like Flight Simulator, as well as The Sims, that Falanghe got into modding, which started him on his journey to game developer. That happened in 2010, while Falanghe was working at the marketing firm Squad, a job he disliked and decided to leave during an intense array of projects: "They said 'If you help us these next couple of months, we'll let you make your game here,'" he recalls. "I was like 'That's not true. That doesn't happen to people … but what do I have to lose?'" The result of this fateful decision was Kerbal Space Program , a unique rocket science simulator that is one of PC Gamer's highest-rated games . "I was always working with this idea that for all I know next week this is over, so let's do anything I can under that assumption," he says. "It would be unthinkable to pitch the entire thing that KSP became to a normal game studio." Falanghe now runs his own development company—Floating Origin Interactive—where he's working on several projects. But he took a break from those to show me around the digital launchpad of his Steam library. We discussed new remakes, old MMOs, and the triumphant return of a PC gaming legend. What game are you currently playing? (Image credit: Bethesda) That would be Oblivion , the remastered version. It's actually been really good. I don't remember playing the original back in the day. I didn't get very far into it. Something else probably grabbed my attention and pulled me away. But I remember feeling really stuck. I just wanted to steal everything I could see, and then I became a vampire by accident. That was problematic. But on the new one, I don't know. Maybe I'm more mature and can understand the story better. Or having played Skyrim and a bunch of Fallouts and Starfield and a bunch of other Bethesda games, going back to Oblivion now, I'm like "Oh yeah, this makes so much more sense now." You can understand the patterns a little better. I'm a stealth archer, of course. Objectively the only correct way to play. The way I play it is maybe less conventional. I have it installed on my main computer here, but I stream it to the Steam Deck and play it on the couch because it's just so much more comfortable …. On the remastered version, I feel like I've finally got a good control setup that uses gamepad controls, so it's like smooth movement and all.
